titre: The Cadbury Report (1992) and the Phrase It Never Wrote
accroche: The Cadbury Report of December 1992 launched “comply or explain”; yet those words do not appear in it, and the code it proposes is not a law.
contenu_vulgarise:
In May 1991, three British institutions (the Financial Reporting Council, the London Stock Exchange, and the accounting profession) create a committee chaired by Sir Adrian Cadbury. The sponsors are concerned, the committee writes, about a low level of confidence in published accounts and in the ability of auditors to provide the safeguards that users expect. On December 1, 1992, the report is published. It is readily summed up by the phrase “comply or explain”: apply the rule or explain yourself. Yet this phrase does not appear in the report.

## A law that is not one

The text proposes a Code of Best Practice, which runs to three pages (pages 58 to 60 of the report). It recommends, for example, separating the roles of chairman and chief executive, or entrusting the audit committee to at least three non-executive directors. But it has no force of law. The committee embraces this: an approach based on a voluntary code coupled with a disclosure requirement will prove, in its view, more effective than a statutory code, because a law would set a minimum and run the risk of having boards follow the letter rather than the spirit.

What gives the code teeth lies elsewhere. The committee recommends that listed companies, for financial years ending after June 30, 1993, state in their annual report whether they comply with the Code and, for any departure, give their reasons. The London Stock Exchange declares that it intends to impose this statement as a continuing listing obligation, and the committee asks that auditors review it before publication. The rule thus never says “comply”: it says “say whether you comply, and why not if you don't.”

## The shift

The received idea is that British corporate governance rests on constraint. The report makes the opposite bet: the constraint applies to information, not to behavior. A company may set aside the separation of the chairman and chief executive roles, provided it says so in black and white and convinces its shareholders. Oversight is entrusted to the market, that is, to those who own the shares.

This choice is not a lukewarm compromise. The committee itself warns that, if companies do not play along, it is likely that legislation and external regulation will be called for. The voluntary code works under the threat of the binding text it claims to avoid.

One question remains that the 1992 report does not settle: is an explanation given in an appendix to an annual report enough for a shareholder who has neither the time nor the means to challenge it?

repere.texte: The Cadbury Committee was set up in May 1991 by the Financial Reporting Council, the London Stock Exchange, and the accounting profession, and its report is dated December 1, 1992.
repere.source: Report of the Committee on the Financial Aspects of Corporate Governance (Cadbury Report), 1992, §2.1 and cover page

carte.punch: “Comply or explain”: the phrase is not in the report that launched it.
carte.idee: The Cadbury Report (1992) does not compel British listed companies to apply its code: it recommends that they say whether they do, and why not if they don't; the London Stock Exchange intends to require it. The constraint applies to information, not to conduct.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: Cadbury Archive, Cambridge Judge Business School: London Stock Exchange letter of July 31, 1992 on the compliance statement
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: Archive document dated July 31, 1992, signed by Sir Andrew Hugh Smith, on the status of the statement of compliance with the Code.

quiz.question: What does the 1992 Cadbury Report make the constraint apply to for listed companies?
choix: Mandatory application of each of the Code's rules, on pain of a fine
The appointment of a regulator in charge of overseeing boards of directors
The annual statement of their compliance with the Code, with the reasons for each departure
A ban on holding directorships in several companies at once
quiz.explication: The committee prefers a voluntary code to a statutory one. What the London Stock Exchange intends to make mandatory, through listing, is to say whether one applies the Code and to justify any departure. The other answers describe constraints on conduct that the report does not impose.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which phrase, often attributed to the Cadbury Report, is actually absent from its text?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The report speaks of stating whether one complies with the Code and giving reasons for departures; the short phrase “comply or explain” does not appear in it. The other three expressions, in English, do appear in the text.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why does the Cadbury committee prefer a voluntary code to a statutory one?
choix: Because a statute would be invalidated by a decision of the London Stock Exchange
Because a law would set a minimum and lead boards to follow the letter rather than the spirit
Because British shareholders reject any form of external regulation
Because Parliament had already passed an equivalent law for banks in 1991
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The report considers that legal measures would impose a minimum and that boards would risk following the letter rather than the spirit, and it warns that legislation would probably be called for if companies did not follow its recommendations.
